candidates.reasoning: Hamming now sells the adaptive-attacker half to banks (FinovateFall, September 2026), and Basware bought Trustpair, the bank-detail validation half, so the old 'drill plus callback' framing has owners on both sides. What is still open is the merged version's core: a deterministic provenance gate at the AP agent's tool boundary (CaMeL-style data-flow policy applied to payee details) plus an automated callback to the number of record, which I found no one selling as an agent-native API. The Basware deal shows strategic acquirers pay for payment-fraud verification, and per-payment checks make it daily infrastructure. It fits the richest posted pot (Hyphenate, $16K) plus Cartesia, Armadin, Nessie and Elastic.
candidates.red_flag: If the pitch leads with red-teaming instead of the provenance gate and callback, it reads as a Hamming clone.

candidates.take: A defensible technique (verified natural-language controls on the write path) in a space where Ramp already applies plain-English policy and review tools already scan the books, so it is a strong Hyphenate entry more than a new company.
candidates.reasoning: Ramp's Policy Agent already turns a written policy into a structured form and applies it to card spend, Xenett lets firms write rule-based review points across clients, and Arden tests SOX controls with agents. None of them advertise the gate itself: rules compiled into a typed language, checked against independent examples and one-edit mutants, and enforced before the write in one serializable transaction. The buyer is real but low-ACV, and the product only works if it owns the path to the bank, which Ramp, BILL and QuickBooks own today. Letting a judge write and then attack their own rule is participatory, but a rules engine is a quieter moment than a ringing phone.
candidates.red_flag: Distribution: the gate must sit on the only path to the bank, and the payment rails already ship policy engines there.

sub.why_now: First Brands (about $2.3B in factoring liabilities; executives charged in Jan 2026 with fabricating invoices and double- and triple-pledging), an April 2026 examiner's report that faults missing independent verification and points to direct buyer-to-financier payment, and UCC Article 12 coming into force (New York June 2026, Ohio Oct 2026).
sub.buyer: Factors and receivables financiers; debtors' AP teams get the gate free
sub.model: Fee per original minted or basis points on financed value
sub.wedge: Mid-size factors that already phone debtors' AP desks to verify invoices before funding
sub.one_liner: A title registry for invoices, so no receivable can be sold twice
sub.wow: On a 3-2-1 count two judges buy the same invoice from their phones; exactly one wins, and every trick the other tries (renumber, split, fake notice of assignment) is refused with the invariant named.

candidates.take: The most novel candidate with the best why-now and a buyer who is scared right now, but the registry binds no one until debtors pay from it.
candidates.reasoning: The legal hooks check out: UCC 12-106 lets an account debtor discharge by paying the current controller, and 9-326A gives a controlling secured party priority over one without control, though adoption varies by state. Existing fixes are fingerprint registries (MonetaGo) and verification services (Iridium Credit, which raised $3M this month to confirm invoices with debtors), and none of them anchor control to the debtor's own PO and receipt or give the AP agent a pay tool with no payee argument. That is exactly the safeguard the First Brands examiner pointed to, so a YC or a16z fintech partner would take the meeting. Two judges racing for one invoice is participatory, but non-finance judges need 20 seconds of setup on factoring.
candidates.red_flag: Two-sided cold start: if debtors keep paying from their vendor master, the registry binds no one, and the race moment can read as a database demo.

candidates.take: A good live phone moment in a crowded, funded category whose vendors already sell 'compliant by design', so a separate gate is better execution, not a new company.
candidates.reasoning: Salient, Domu, Prodigal and Skit.ai all sell AI collection agents with compliance as the headline, and Sedric monitors collections compliance. Vendor playbooks already describe this exact design: identity verification before any disclosure, the 7-in-7 cap enforced in the dialer policy layer, and hard-coded Mini-Miranda audio. The rules themselves check out (12 CFR 1006.14 frequency presumptions; the FCC's 2024 AI-voice ruling), and a vendor-neutral gate sold for bank due diligence is a plausible wedge. candidates.red_flag: Every funded AI collector already claims deterministic guardrails, so 'why would Salient's customers buy a second gate?' has no sharp answer.

picks.why: Highest score through my lens: the best live moment, the richest posted pot and a per-payment product whose acquirer market Basware just proved; lead with the provenance gate and callback, not red-teaming.

The most novel candidate with the strongest why-now (First Brands charges, the examiner's report, UCC Article 12) and a buyer who is scared right now; the only challenger I would fund ahead of Netting House.

verdict_vs_leaders: No. Original Bill (CH2, 7.0) and Controls CI (CH6, 7.0) beat Netting House (6.7) through my lens, but no challenger beats Fire Drill (7.3).
ceo_note: Stay on Fire Drill, but the ground moved since round 1: Hamming showed an adaptive bank red team at FinovateFall in September and Basware bought Trustpair, so open with the provenance gate plus callback and name both before a judge does. If you want a real alternative rather than another Fire Drill variant, Original Bill is the one a YC partner would lean in on: First Brands is the biggest receivables fraud in years, Iridium Credit raised $3M this month on a narrower version, and in states that adopted Article 12 the UCC already says paying the controller discharges the debt. Drop Reg F Gate; every funded AI collector already sells deterministic compliance.
